extracted.intended_audience: writers, readers, and students interested in character, moral philosophy, and social manners (creative writers, literary critics, general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles about what constitutes moral 'character' and social 'manners' in persons and writing — useful for creators aiming to portray convincing, commanding personalities and for critics assessing them. Emphasis is on presence, authenticity, inner source of action, and the distinction between appearance and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as reserved force/presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is 'a reserved force which acts directly by presence, and without means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson explains that character operates by immediate presence rather than by a catalogue of deeds; it is latent and often independent of speech or explicit action. Good portrayals should show a figure whose mere arrival 'alters the face of affairs' and whose influence is conveyed by presence more than by narrative of acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation may exceed recorded deeds (latent greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many great men seem to possess something 'finer in the man than any thing which he said' — an element that 'begot an expectation that outran all their performance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing greatness, allow for an impression of incomputable latent power — suggest hints and aura rather than only enumerated achievements. Characters can be made credible by implying depths that facts alone do not capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character makes talent trusted (authenticity/faith in a fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The people need more than talent; they need 'the power to make his talent trusted' — a person 'invincibly persuaded' of a fact in himself so that others' impudence and terror are wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals should show inner conviction and authenticity. A convincing character embodies and signals a truth so clearly that others infer reliability from their presence and demeanor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest by demonstration rather than force
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men 'conquer because his arrival alters the face of affairs' — victories 'by demonstration of superiority, and not by crossing of bayonets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative, give characters convincing moral or intellectual superiority that sways others without explicit conflict; show subtle dominance — presence, composure, and moral weight — instead of only physical action or rhetorical flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fronting the fact; original perception over secondhand thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of fronting the fact, and not dealing with it at second hand through someone else's perceptions, is essential to natural greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be shown engaging with reality directly — decisive perception and immediate relation to facts — rather than parroting received opinions. In writing, avoid characters who merely echo others; give them primary convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural probity and insight as foundations of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in fields like trade rests in the man: 'His natural probity combines with his insight into the fabric of society' making him above tricks and inspiring respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict enterprise and competence as rooted in character: honesty, steady judgment, and a sense of public equity. Avoid portraying skill as purely technical; link it to moral temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate vocation (some things cannot be learned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some persons 'must be born to trade or he cannot learn it' — certain faculties are native and not wholly acquirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing mastery, consider inborn temperament and bearing; portray limits where characters attempt tasks beyond their natural capacity to show authenticity and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence as an almost physical force
rubrics_metrics.description: Character exerts an influence 'like light and heat' that 'runs down from his eyes into all those who beheld him' and can 'benumb' or overwhelm others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show influence as contagious and embodied. Scenes can convey how a character's presence changes others' behavior and feeling — a quiet command that reshapes a room without speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as conduit of truth and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is the summit of being; justice is its application; 'the will of the pure runs down from them into other natures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray moral clarity as intrinsic, not merely ideological. Characters of high character function as moral centers whose sense of justice naturally affects those around them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual as encloser — infusing the world with personal quality
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual is 'an encloser' who 'animates all he can, and he sees only what he animates' — he encloses the world as material basis for his character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization should show how a person's inner temperament colors their perception and transforms environment; the world they inhabit reflects their disposition rather than being neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of character is resistance of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural measure of power is the resistance of circumstances; rectitude 'is a perpetual victory, celebrated not by cries of joy but by serenity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test characters by the difficulties they face. True character manifests in steadiness and serenity under pressure, not in triumphal displays. Portray resilience and moral calm as markers of depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding dependence on events for self-worth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is disgraceful to 'fly to events for confirmation of our truth and worth' — prosperity or circumstance cannot repair defect of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should derive identity from internal convictions, not ephemeral successes. In plotting and characterization, resist defining people solely by external achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficingness and sense of mass (centrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The face which character wears is 'self-sufficingness' — 'a sense of mass' that makes a man seem permanent and not displaced by fortune or exile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray major figures as solid, centered presences whose comportment suggests inner resources. Tone, posture, and calm speech can signal this quality in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of nonconformity and 'uncivil' independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonconformity and being 'uncivil, unavailable' can be socially useful by provoking thought and resisting easy acquiescence to establishment opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show principled dissent and refusal to pander as virtues. Characters who resist consensus — even awkwardly — can function as provocateurs who elevate moral discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must rest on substance; be equal to one's enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Our action should 'rest mathematically on our substance' — attempt nothing beyond one's real force; institutions cannot exceed their founders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plausibility: characters' deeds should flow from demonstrable capacities. Avoid deus ex machina heroics — greatness ought to be grounded in the character's established qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incessant growth and forward-looking earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should be 'intelligent and earnest' and show 'a controlling happy future opening before them' — new actions are the only apologies and explanations of old ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict characters as developing, aspiring, and forward-moving. Show growth through new actions that recontextualize past behavior, and avoid static portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence as inexhaustible and not merely enumerable
rubrics_metrics.description: True benevolence cannot be accounted for by a list of transactions; 'Love is inexhaustible' and the measure of a man's charity is not crowd-sourcable by receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey generosity as habitual spirit rather than a ledger of good deeds. Small, repeated acts and an overall disposition of giving dramatize genuine benevolence better than lists of donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character cannot be successfully imitated
rubrics_metrics.description: Character 'is nature in the highest form. It is of no use to ape it or to contend with it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid caricature and surface mimicry when depicting depth. Authenticity comes from inner coherence, not from copied mannerisms or rhetorical posturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seclusion and unspoiled development of great natures
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatly-destined should 'slip up into life in the shade' — nature keeps these sovereignties in her own hands, and solitude protects the growth of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show some geniuses or noble characters as developing privately, insulated from public flattery; their emergence should feel organic and unmanufactured by society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine persons are unique and resist ready comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Great 'divine persons' are 'character born' and 'Nature never rhymes her children' — they disappoint predictions and require perspective to apprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting exceptional characters, avoid forcing analogies to historical figures; allow uniqueness and unexpected directions rather than predictable arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship grounded in character — profound mutual confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict relations of amity rooted in character produce 'the profound good understanding' which is more satisfying than politics or commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray friendships as moral and spiritual affinities that reveal character; moments of mutual confidence and unforced generosity dramatize the moral quality of characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of presence and the singular moment in relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'moment is all, in all noble relations' — an unexpected meeting can pause life's hurry and magnify significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes of sudden encounter and concentrated presence to reveal depth of relation; brief shared moments can be more telling than lengthy explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman as composite of spirit and incommunicable properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is a 'spontaneous fruit of talents and feelings' — a compound result of virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, and power, made of spirit more than talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting refined social figures, focus on inner disposition and integrated qualities rather than merely on external trappings of fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman as truth-teller and lord of his actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions, and expressing that lordship in his behavior, not in any manner dependent and servile' — 'manhood first, and then gentleness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character creation, emphasize autonomy, moral integrity, and benevolence together. Manners should flow from truthfulness and self-command, not from affectation or servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fashion from substantive manners
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish between fashion (narrow, often sinister) and the heroic character the gentleman imports; 'appearance supposes a substance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating elegant surface with genuine gentility. In writing, show manners that reveal inner worth rather than empty polish; contrast superficial fashion with deep courtesy.
